definition: Lethargic means sluggish and lacking energy.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word lethargic. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know lethargic should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The flu left Amara lethargic for a week, and even lifting the kettle felt like a chore worth planning.
Tired is the everyday rung, well below lethargic — a good night's sleep cures tired.
Sluggish comes closer but stops short of lethargic — sluggish slows your morning, while lethargic drags at the whole day and will not lift.

Listless is the mood side of low energy: no interest, no spark, nothing seems worth wanting. Lethargic is the body's side — sluggish limbs, slow responses, every action costing more than it should. A listless patient pushes the tray away uninterested; a lethargic one can barely lift the fork.

Drowsy means heavy with sleep specifically — the eyelids dropping, a nap about to win. Lethargic is a broader, longer drain: days of flat, low energy that a night's sleep doesn't fix. Drowsiness lifts once you finally rest; lethargy hangs on through rest and after it.

bright, bouncy, and quick to move

Greek lethe ('forgetfulness') left no other common English word — even 'lethal' is a false friend, from Latin letum ('death'), not from forgetting. Lethe itself survives only as the name of the mythical river whose water washed memory away.
Lethargic means sluggish and lacking energy.
Nobody warned the new keeper about February at the reptile house: the iguanas go lethargic in the short days, draping their branches like wet towels and stirring only when the heat lamps cycle on.
Lethargic describes energy at low tide — sluggish in body, slow to stir, every action costing more than it should.
It runs deeper than 'tired': a nap fixes tired, while lethargy hangs on, dragging at the whole system.
Lethargic is the word doctors and vets reach for: a flat, lasting energy drain, often a symptom.
Use 'tired' for what sleep will fix and 'sluggish' for a slow patch; call someone lethargic when the battery itself seems drained — days of it, not hours.

The wildlife center's staff noticed the change in the young otter within days of her rescue.
She had arrived thin but bright; now she drifted through her pool in slow motion, and keepers logged her as lethargic in the morning notes.
Extra sleep didn't touch it.
Keepers dimmed the lights, lengthened her nights, and found her just as heavy and slow the next day.
Bloodwork found the culprit: a parasite quietly draining her strength week after week.
Two rounds of treatment later, the morning crew clocked her at nineteen ramp climbs before breakfast.
